papers.title: A divergent bat orthopneumovirus with zoonotic potential constrained by RSV adaptive immunity and broad-spectrum treatment.
papers.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; genus Orthopneumovirus ) causes severe pneumonia in young children worldwide, yet the zoonotic potential of the few known nonhuman animal orthopneumoviruses remains unknown. Here, we characterized a highly divergent bat orthopneumovirus (BPV) from West African straw-colored fruit bats and established a systematic framework for evaluating zoonotic risk posed by an emerging viral pathogen. Epidemiologic data in bats showed a low viral detection rate (24 of 1778 RT-PCR positive) and low seroprevalence (6 of 66 IgG IFA positive), suggesting BPV episodic circulation potentially sustained in immunologically naïve bats following bat birthing events. Near-complete genomes from two BPV genetic variants revealed prototypic orthopneumovirus organization, but lacked the SH viroporin-encoding gene present in RSV. Functional experiments showed that BPV NS1/NS2 antagonized human interferon β responses, and that BPV pseudoviruses entered human cells (4.5- to 53.5-fold less efficiently than RSV), while being cross-neutralized by human RSV-reactive antisera, together suggesting zoonotic traits that may be partly constrained by cross-protective immunity. BPV escaped neutralization by RSV-specific therapeutic palivizumab and inhibition by lonafarnib, but remained susceptible to MPE8, a broad-spectrum monoclonal antibody that targets the conserved pneumovirus antigenic site III. These findings identify zoonotic traits of a divergent bat pneumovirus while suggesting potential protective value of preexisting RSV immunity and broad-spectrum interventions, which has implications for pandemic preparedness. Whether cross-protection in the human population may change by the advent of RSV vaccination warrants investigation. Efforts to investigate orthopneumovirus host shifts, reservoir studies, and development of broadly reactive orthopneumovirus vaccines and antivirals are warranted.

papers.title: MdVQ24 orchestrates apple immunity against Botryosphaeria dothidea in a VQ domain-dependent manner via MdWRKY31-mediated transcriptional repression.
papers.abstract: Apple ring rot caused by Botryosphaeria dothidea severely restricts apple sustainable production. VQ proteins act as transcriptional co-regulators in plant stress immunity, yet their roles and the functional mechanism of conserved VQ domains in apple resistance to this pathogen remain largely unclear. VQ proteins typically interact with WRKY transcription factors to modulate downstream defense genes, but the structural basis of VQ-WRKY binding and its immune regulatory output in woody fruit trees lack systematic verification. This study aimed to identify key VQ gene conferring apple ring rot resistance, clarify the indispensable function of the VQ domain, and dissect the molecular regulatory module underlying MdVQ24-mediated immunity. Transcriptome screening obtained MdVQ24 induced by pathogen. Transient fruit transformation, stable transgenic apple seedlings and calli verified its disease resistance function. Y2H, pull-down, BiFC, LCI confirmed protein interaction; site-directed mutagenesis, molecular docking, EMSA, LUC/GUS assays analyzed VQ domain structural function; ROS staining, antioxidant enzyme and secondary metabolite detection characterized immune phenotypes. MdVQ24 was nucleus-localized and strongly pathogen-induced. Its overexpression enhanced resistance while silencing weakened immunity. MdVQ24 bound MdWRKY31 via VQ domain α-helix; V 70 /Q 71 mutation destroyed helix conformation, abolished interaction and lost capacity to strengthen MdWRKY31 repression on negative immune regulator MdHIR4. Mutant transient overexpression failed to activate ROS burst, callose deposition and defense gene expression, with lesion areas equivalent to control. MdVQ24-conferred resistance is partially dependent on MdWRKY31. MdVQ24 positively regulates apple ring rot resistance through an MdVQ24-MdWRKY31-MdHIR4 module. The intact VQ domain with conserved V 70 /Q 71 residues is a structural and functional prerequisite for protein interaction and immune activation. This work reveals the structure-function relationship of VQ proteins and provides target genes for disease-resistant apple breeding.

papers.title: From digital pathology to integrated precision oncology: AI-driven biomarker assessment and multimodal data integration in non-small cell lung cancer.
papers.abstract: Digital pathology (DP) is evolving from an image-based diagnostic modality into a quantitative platform for computational precision oncology. This transition is particularly relevant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), where limited tissue specimens must support histological classification, immunohistochemistry, broad molecular profiling and an expanding range of therapy-linked biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI) can assist conventional tasks such as tissue segmentation, cell detection, quality control and biomarker quantification, but it can also derive image-based signatures associated with molecular alterations, spatial immune organization and treatment response. This review focuses primarily on NSCLC and examines the continuum from foundational image-analysis tasks and AI-assisted PD-L1 scoring to histology-based molecular prediction, computational companion diagnostics, pathology foundation models and multimodal AI. We discuss recent lung-specific evidence, including computational triage of actionable alterations, the emerging TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring paradigm and selected protein biomarkers associated with antibody-drug conjugates. We also consider the integration of pathology with genomics, transcriptomics, liquid biopsy, radiology and longitudinal clinical data. Particular attention is given to the barriers separating algorithmic performance from clinical utility: uneven adoption of whole-slide imaging, pre-analytical and scanner variability, missing or asynchronous multimodal data, propagation of upstream measurement errors, laboratory information-system interoperability, prospective validation, regulation, reimbursement and equitable access. Emerging paradigms such as digital twins and agentic AI are discussed as research directions rather than established clinical tools. We argue that the principal value of AI in NSCLC will not be autonomous diagnosis, but the reliable conversion of fragmented data streams into transparent, auditable and clinically actionable patient representations.

papers.title: TSG-01 in the treatment of chronic heart failure in patients with coronary artery disease: A prospective clinical phase IIa trial.
papers.abstract: TSG-01, a novel agent dominated by secondary ginsenosides, may benefit chronic heart failure (CHF), yet its efficacy and safety in CHF patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) remain unclear. This phase IIa trial enrolled 85 CAD patients with NYHA III CHF (40-75 years), randomized to high-dose TSG-01 (n=29), low-dose TSG-01 (n=28), or placebo (n=28) for 12 weeks. Outcomes were evaluated in the intention-to-treat cohort (ITT, n=85) and an exploratory digoxin-free cohort (n=59). No significant between-group difference was found for the NYHA-based efficacy endpoint. In the ITT cohort, only low-dose TSG-01 significantly improved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) versus placebo; in the digoxin-free cohort, both doses yielded significant LVEF improvement. Diseases occurring the infectious and infective system, gastrointestinal system and the blood and lymphatic system are the common adverse events, with no significant difference between the 3 groups. Together, this study demonstrates that TSG-01 is well tolerated with similar adverse event profiles across groups, and confers potential cardiac benefits in digoxin-free patients, warranting further confirmatory studies. Registration: Clinicaltrials.gov, no. NCT04515290.

papers.title: ILAE genetic literacy series: Variant interpretation in epilepsy.
papers.abstract: This article is the first in a two-part primer on variant interpretation in epilepsies, as part of the Genetic Literacy Series by the Genetics Commission of the International League Against Epilepsy. Advances in genetics have significantly improved our understanding of epilepsy, but challenges remain in interpreting the clinical relevance of identified variants. As diagnostic approaches shift from targeted gene panels to broader methods like exome and genome sequencing (ES/GS), the volume of detected variants continues to grow. This primer provides a practical guide to help clinicians navigate variant interpretation, focusing on key aspects such as variant frequency, inheritance, and genotype-phenotype correlations. By equipping clinicians with this knowledge, we aim to improve the integration of genomic testing into routine epilepsy care and enhance patient outcomes. This primer introduces genetic testing strategies, explores the evidence framework for variant interpretation, and concludes by examining common challenges and a case resolution.

papers.title: Development of an indirect ELISA method based on the PDCoV S1 protein and evaluation of its correlation with serum neutralization test.
papers.abstract: Porcine deltacoronavirus (PDCoV) is an emerging enteric pathogen and poses a significant threat to the global swine industry, necessitating reliable serological tools for both diagnosis and protective immunity assessment. Most current PDCoV antibody detection methods target the viral nucleocapsid (N) protein; however, these assays primarily detect non-neutralizing antibodies and correlate poorly with protective immunity. In this study, we developed an indirect ELISA (S1-iELISA) using a consensus S1 antigen (S1-Con) designed from 34 PDCoV strains across multiple lineages and expressed in CHO-K1 cells to preserve native conformational epitopes. Following systematic optimization of coating concentration, antibody dilutions, and reaction conditions, the S1-iELISA was validated using 247 swine serum samples. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.9959, with a diagnostic sensitivity of 97.89% and specificity of 98.10% at the optimal cut-off (S/P = 0.25). The assay exhibited excellent repeatability (intra-assay CV: 0.76% to 7.18%; inter-assay CV: 1.17% to 8.74%) and no cross-reactivity with other major porcine pathogens. Importantly, the S1-iELISA results demonstrated a strong positive correlation with those of the serum neutralization test (Spearman r = 0.9762, p < 0.001). In conclusion, this S1-iELISA represents a promising serological tool for evaluating neutralizing antibody levels, providing a robust tool for PDCoV epidemiological surveillance, vaccine efficacy assessment, and population-level immune monitoring.

papers.title: Elucidating the molecular interplay between nicotine and ankylosing spondylitis: an integrated systems toxicology study.
papers.abstract: This study aims to investigate the potential effects and underlying mechanisms of nicotine on ankylosing spondylitis(AS). Potential targets of nicotine were predicted using the CTD. Gene targets for AS were retrieved from four public databases. Protein-protein interaction network and pathway enrichment analysis were performed. Subsequently, we constructed seven machine learning models using the GSE73754 dataset to identify diagnostic biomarkers. Molecular docking was performed to predict binding affinities and modes, complemented by molecular dynamics simulations for detailed interactions and conformational changes. Lastly, we conducted an in silico knockout experiment using the GSE232131 dataset for validation. After systematic screening of multiple databases, we identified 38 overlapping targets between nicotine and AS. Network analysis refined these to eight hub targets. Enrichment analysis highlighted their significant involvement in inflammatory and immune-related processes, particularly the IL-17 and NF-κB signaling pathway. The logistic regression model exhibited the best predictive performance (AUC 0.905). Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations revealed stable binding complexes, especially with TNF, IL1B and IL10. A virtual knockout experiment revealed TNF as a critical gene within the interaction network. This study provides computational evidence on nicotine's potential impact on AS development. It establishes a foundation for further research on AS preventive and therapeutic strategies. Moreover, the reproducible computational pipeline established can be readily adapted to investigate other environmental triggers in autoimmune diseases and inform the development of evidence-based public health policies related to nicotine exposure.

papers.title: One-Pot Assembly of Porphyrin-Gold Nanostructures with Enhanced Photothermal Response toward Biomedical Applications.
papers.abstract: A simple aqueous one-pot strategy was developed for the direct preparation of gold-porphyrin nanoassemblies (AuNPs@por) using an amino-functionalized porphyrin as an active molecular building block. Unlike conventional postsynthetic conjugation approaches, the porphyrin contributed to nanoparticle organization during NaBH4-mediated reduction, enabling the rapid formation of hybrid nanostructures under mild conditions. Systematic variation of the reducing-agent amount showed that, whereas bare gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) displayed tunable size and surface characteristics, the presence of the porphyrin promoted their organization into compact, positively charged nanoassemblies with reproducible structural features. The optimized formulation exhibited long-term colloidal stability (>6 months), high porphyrin loading (30 ± 0.5 μmol g-1), and retention of the characteristic optical signature of the free-base porphyrin, confirming its effective incorporation while preserving its optical properties. The resulting proof-of-concept platform was readily biofunctionalized with PNA and DNA model probes through electrostatic interactions, preserving colloidal stability and molecular-recognition capability while improving hemocompatibility. Under 532 nm laser irradiation, AuNPs@por exhibited an enhanced photothermal response compared with bare AuNPs (ΔT up to 8.5 °C vs 3.2 °C). Furthermore, ex vivo irradiation of human oral squamous cell carcinoma tissue induced localized morphological alterations consistent with a predominantly photothermal effect, supporting the light-to-heat conversion capability of the hybrid nanoassemblies.

papers.title: Comparative pan-genomics reveals extensive variation in secondary metabolism and the non-coding repertoire of clinically relevant Fusarium solani species complex members.
papers.abstract: The Fusarium solani species complex (FSSC) is a group of dual-kingdom fungal pathogens capable of causing devastating disease on a wide range of host plants and life-threatening infections in humans that are difficult to treat. In this study, we generate highly contiguous genomes for three clinical isolates each of Fusarium keratoplasticum and Fusarium petroliphilum and compare them with others of the FSSC from plant and animal sources. We find no clear host specialization within the complex, with isolates from plant and animal sources being intermixed on the phylogeny. Pangenome analysis revealed extensive gene presence-absence, with only 41% of genes found in all samples and accessory chromosomes encoding isolate- and species-specific genes. Definition of long non-coding RNAs in F. keratoplasticum and F. petroliphilum demonstrated that they show a similarly high degree of presence-absence variation but are integrated into the transcriptional network to a similar degree as protein-coding genes, suggesting broad and extensive cellular roles, including secondary metabolism. Finally, examination of the FSSC for gigantic Starship mobile genetic elements revealed that two-thirds of the samples analyzed harbored at least one element. However, the cargo contained within these elements was largely isolate-specific, highlighting their role in contributing to the high degree of gene content variation observed. This study provides valuable insights into the evolutionary dynamics and genomic architecture of the FSSC, with implications for understanding its generalist nature and multi-kingdom virulence, something of increasing relevance as climate change potentially increases the number of fungal species that can grow at human temperatures.IMPORTANCEThe Fusarium solani species complex is a group of fungi capable of destroying important crops and causing human infections that are often antifungal resistant. While the magnitude of disease in both the plant and animal kingdom is apparent, we are currently lacking a data set to characterize the genomic diversity that likely underpins its fitness in such different hosts. This study generates six highly contiguous clinical genomes of F. keratoplasticum and F. petroliphilum and compares them against other Fusarium solani species complex members, finding tremendous differences in gene content between isolates and species. Through definition of the secondary metabolic potential, long non-coding RNAs, and Starship mobile genetic elements, we begin to unravel the forces that cause such tremendous genetic diversity, and their potential consequences for both human and plant infection.

papers.title: Volumetric Digital Microsphere Assay Coupling CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a and Lens-Free Holography for Salmonella typhimurium Detection.
papers.abstract: Sensitive and precise quantification of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices remains challenging due to inefficient signal conversion, limited volumetric information, and inaccurate counting under dense signal conditions. Here, we develop an integrated digital biosensing platform that combines programmable biochemical amplification, lens-free holographic imaging, and intelligent computational decoding. A CbAgo-CRISPR/Cas12a cascade is employed to convert pathogen DNA signals into discrete microsphere-based digital outputs, while automated lens-free holography preserves three-dimensional spatial information for high-throughput acquisition. A depth-guided Transformer algorithm further enables accurate three-dimensional microsphere localization in dense sensing environments. Using Salmonella typhimurium as a model pathogen, the platform exhibited a linear response from 20 to 107 CFU/mL with a detection limit of 12 CFU/mL. The method showed good selectivity against the tested nontarget bacteria and was further evaluated in spiked chicken, egg, fish, and milk matrices, yielding quantitative results in good agreement with conventional plate counting. These results demonstrate a particle-based volumetric transduction strategy for digital biosensing in complex samples.

papers.title: Utilization of an Activity-Based Probe to Explore Interactomes of DXP Synthase.
papers.abstract: During infection, bacteria rapidly adapt to evade the host immune response, enduring nutrient limitation and other harsh conditions. To aid adaptation, bacteria have evolved multifunctional proteins capable of sensing environmental changes and modulating signaling and enzyme activity in response to host-derived stresses. We hypothesize that the bacterial central metabolic enzyme 1-deoxy-d-xylulose 5-phosphate synthase (DXPS) is multifunctional: in its canonical role, DXPS catalyzes the synthesis of DXP via a ThDP-dependent ligand-gated mechanism using pyruvate and d-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (d-GAP); additionally, it exhibits species-specific alternative activities and structural/mechanistic features, suggesting bacteria exploit DXPS in distinct ways to survive in different infection contexts. Here, we demonstrate ABP 1, an acetyl phosphonate activity-based probe, as a tool to interrogate species-specific DXPS inhibition and function. We found that DXPS homologs with low sequence similarity are comparably inhibited/labeled by ABP 1, and competitive activity-based protein profiling using ABP 1 allows detection of species-specific inhibitor potencies. Crosslinking of ABP 1 to DXPS maintains the enzyme as the dimer in a closed conformation. Intriguingly, pulldown experiments using immobilized E. coli or P. aeruginosa PAO1 DXPS-ABP 1 adducts with matching lysates (E. coli MG1655 or PAO1) suggest a broader role for DXPS in metabolism/cellular regulation in bacteria and the potential for pathogen-specific DXPS functions. These findings establish ABP 1-enabled pulldowns as a platform to explore DXPS multifunctionality and identify pathogen-specific DXPS-protein complexes, opening avenues to explore DXPS biology and for the development of antibacterial strategies targeting pathogen-specific DXPS functions.

papers.title: From Emerging Vectors to Missed Fevers: Why Fragile Health Systems Need Integrated Fever-Vector Preparedness.
papers.abstract: Climate change, urbanization, population mobility, and expanding mosquito vectors are reshaping infectious-disease risks in fragile health systems, where surveillance, diagnosis, and response often remain fragmented. This Policy Analysis argues that preparedness should move beyond isolated pathogen- or vector-specific programs toward an integrated fever-vector model. Undifferentiated fever should serve as the clinical entry point linking environmental intelligence, entomological surveillance, sentinel fever surveillance, tiered laboratory testing, and public health response. Such integration could improve recognition of arboviral infections overlooked in malaria-centered systems, support earlier outbreak detection, and guide targeted vector control and diagnostic preparedness. Somalia and the wider Horn of Africa illustrate the urgency of this shift because climate shocks, displacement, weak laboratory systems, and emerging urban vector-borne risks increasingly converge. The priority is not a more technologically complex system, but a connected and sustainable preparedness architecture capable of linking emerging vectors with febrile illnesses presenting in routine care.

papers.title: GSH/pH Dual-Responsive Zwitterionic mRNA Nanocomplexes for Tumor-Enriched mRNA Delivery in a B16F10 Melanoma Model.
papers.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapy offers a programmable route to melanoma treatment, but its translation is limited by nuclease degradation, off-target biodistribution and endolysosomal trapping. Here we report a glutathione (GSH)/pH dual-responsive mRNA nanocomplex (mRNA-NC) fabricated by one-pot in situ polymerization of N-(3-aminopropyl)methacrylamide (APMA), 1-vinylimidazole (VI), N,N'-bis(acryloyl)cystamine (BACA), and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine (MPC) on the mRNA template. At an N/P ratio of 40, the carrier reached an encapsulation efficiency of 92.7 ± 2.1% and a loading capacity of 87.4 ± 3.2 μg mg-1, forming monodisperse particles of 126.4 ± 7.2 nm (polydispersity index, PDI, 0.14). The zwitterionic corona limited plasma protein adsorption to 12.6 ± 1.5 μg mg-1 (4.6-fold lower than jetPEI/mRNA), kept hemolysis at 0.8 ± 0.2%, and extended the serum half-life of the mRNA to ≈27.4 h, roughly 9-fold longer than naked mRNA. Release was gated by both triggers: 86.5 ± 3.7% of the cargo was released within 8 h under 10 mM GSH, whereas leakage under physiological conditions remained ≤ 12%; in a 4 h matrix, pH 5.5 plus 10 mM GSH released 85 ± 6.8% versus 12 ± 1.5% at pH 7.4 without GSH. In B16F10 cells, the nanocomplex was taken up in a dose- and energy-dependent manner, entered the lysosomal compartment, and escaped over time in a manner consistent with imidazole-mediated proton-sponge buffering (a hypothesis; intralysosomal pH was not measured directly), producing a peak firefly luciferase (FLuc) expression of 56,140 ± 3280 RLU mg-1 protein at 24 h, about 1.5-fold higher than jetPEI/mRNA, with 93.6 ± 3.9% cell viability and 6.7 ± 1.2% lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release. In B16F10-bearing albino C57BL/6 mice, a single intravenous dose produced tumor-dominant bioluminescence (peak 5.7 × 106 photons s-1 at 6 h), a tumor enrichment index of 1.22 ± 0.18 (vs 0.31 ± 0.03 for jetPEI/mRNA) and 2.42 × 107 FLuc mRNA copies μg-1 tumor RNA at 12 h, while all 7-day safety indicators remained at phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) levels. These results demonstrate that a single zwitterionic nanocomplex can integrate stealth, dual-triggered release, and endosomal escape for safe, tumor-enriched mRNA delivery. While this study focuses on delivery performance and reporter gene expression, it lays a solid foundation for future therapeutic applications with functional mRNA.

papers.title: Evolution, application and clinical significance of profiling chromatin interactions at a genome-wide scale.
papers.abstract: Over the past few decades, chromatin biology has evolved from viewing chromatin as a static structural scaffold to decoding it as a dynamic, programmable regulatory landscape. At the heart of this transformation is the precise mapping of interactions between functional proteins and cognate DNA elements. Although high-throughput technologies have generated comprehensive atlases of these genomic features, the field is now transitioning from descriptive mapping to mechanistic elucidation, paving the way for predictive diagnostics and target therapeutics. Here, we review the conceptual and methodological evolution of chromatin-protein interaction profiling, tracing the history from classical biochemical footprints to single-cell multi-omic integration. We reason that specific chromatin-protein interactions may serve as key structural linchpins organizing 3D genome architecture. By coupling single-cell multi-omics with functional perturbation, we illustrate how to move beyond observational correlations to establish direct causal links connecting chromatin architecture, epigenetic modifications, and transcriptional outputs. Ultimately, we conceptualize "Sentinel Genomics", an emerging paradigm leveraging these multi-layered chromatin insights to forecast disease trajectories and therapeutic responses well before clinical manifestation.

papers.title: Novel Nonradioactive Molecular Hybridization Strategies for the Sensitive Detection of Plant Viruses: Carnation Mottle Virus as a Case Study.
papers.abstract: Rapid and sensitive detection of plant viruses is essential for effective disease management. Nonradioactive molecular hybridization using digoxigenin-labeled riboprobes is a robust diagnostic method; however, its sensitivity can limit early virus detection. Here, we report two complementary strategies to improve assay performance using carnation mottle virus (CarMV) as a proof-of-concept model. First, we evaluate the tandem cloning of multiple genomic fragments from a single virus, adapting the polyprobe concept to monovalent detection. Second, we introduce a novel double-hybridization (DH) system in which unlabeled primary probes carrying a common tail hybridize to the target RNA, and a labeled secondary probe binds to the shared tail. When tested on serial dilutions of infected plant extracts, both systems enhance the sensitivity five-fold compared with a conventional single probe. Using full-length CarMV transcripts, the optimized DH system shows the lowest limit of detection: 1.9 × 10 5 molecules/μl, corresponding to approximately 400 fg of viral RNA. This represents a 25-fold improvement over a conventional probe and approaches the sensitivity of RT-PCR. Both strategies reported here enhance assay sensitivity, strengthening the diagnostic potential of nonradioactive molecular hybridization. In particular, the DH system provides a streamlined and adaptable platform for developing sensitive polyvalent assays without the constraints of traditional polyprobe engineering. In addition, the estimated cost of molecular hybridization was only 0.03 to 0.04€ per sample per pathogen, which is substantially lower than that of other commonly used detection methods. Collectively, these improvements represent a practical advance for diagnostic laboratories and large-scale plant virus surveillance programs.

papers.title: Molecular diagnostic testing variation and outcomes in pediatric complicated pneumonia.
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is estimated to cause <10% of pediatric complicated community-acquired pneumonia (cCAP) cases, yet >70% receive empiric methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA)-directed antibiotics. Molecular diagnostic testing (MDT) improves pathogen detection compared with culture; however, its impact on antibiotic stewardship and outcomes remains unclear. To (1) describe national variation in MDT use among children hospitalized with cCAP and (2) compare length of stay (LOS), MRSA-directed antibiotic exposure, and costs across testing strategies. We conducted a retrospective study of children 2 months to 18 years of age hospitalized with cCAP (2021-2024) using the Pediatric Health Information System database. MDT was classified as broad-array (multiplex polymerase chain reaction [PCR] or sequencing-based modalities) or single-target (PCR assays for Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus). Because culture use was nearly universal, hospitals were grouped by high versus low broad-array and single-target MDT use, generating four groups via K-means clustering. Generalized estimating equations assessed associations between testing group and outcomes, adjusting for payor, intensive care unit admission, and illness severity. Among 2994 hospitalizations at 43 hospitals, 98.5% had blood or pleural cultures, 26.2% broad-array MDT, and 44.2% single-target MDT. MRSA-directed antibiotic use ranged from 67% to 93% across the four groups. Compared with hospitals with low broad-array/low single-target MDT, those with low broad-array/high single-target MDT use had lower MRSA-directed antibiotic exposure (risk ratio [RR]: 0.34, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.17-0.67; p = .002). LOS and costs did not differ among groups. Low broad-array/high single-target MDT use was associated with reduced MRSA-directed antibiotic exposure without differences in LOS or costs. Prospective studies should evaluate MDT-guided antibiotic optimization.

papers.title: From Expanded Carrier Screening to Dynamic and Personalised Preconceptional Genomics.
papers.abstract: Expanded carrier screening (ECS) has substantially broadened the scope of preconception genetic screening, but the expansion of fixed gene panels has also highlighted important limitations related to population diversity, genomic coverage, variant interpretation, residual risk and the clinical value of increasingly large panels. Recent advances in population genomics, sequencing technologies, longitudinal variant reassessment, quantitative risk assessment and artificial intelligence (AI) provide opportunities to move beyond static screening models. This review examines current challenges in ECS and explores the transition towards a more dynamic and individualised framework for preconceptional genomics. Rather than continually expanding fixed panels, genomic information could be selectively interpreted within the reproductive context and reassessed as knowledge, variant classifications and individual circumstances evolve. Emerging technologies, including exome- and long-read sequencing and AI-assisted variant interpretation, may facilitate this transition, although limitations related to validation, population diversity, penetrance and clinical interpretation remain. Genetic counselling and professional oversight will therefore remain essential to ensure that increasingly complex genomic information is translated into meaningful reproductive risk assessment and informed reproductive decision-making.

papers.title: Prokaryotic community structure, functional traits, and potential pathogens in a multi-stage waste stabilization pond system.
papers.abstract: Waste stabilization ponds (WSPs) are widely used for wastewater treatment in low-resource settings, the structure of prokaryotic communities and the attenuation of potential pathogens in full-scale systems remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the prokaryotic community structure, predicted functional profiles, and environmental drivers across a full-scale WSP system in Egypt. Forty-eight water samples were collected over one year four sampling points along the treatment train: inlet, anaerobic pond, facultative pond, and final outlet. Samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and physicochemical profiling. Prokaryotic communities showed distinct spatial structuring among sampling points, with most pairwise comparisons showing strong separation (PERMANOVA R² > 0.3, p < 0.001), accompanied by sampling point-associated differences in alpha diversity, including significantly lower diversity in the anaerobic pond than in the other sampling points. Linear discrimination analysis (LDA) revealed sampling points-specific biomarkers, highlighting Firmicutes in the inlet, Gammaproteobacteria in the anaerobic pond, and Actinobacteriota in the outlet, reflecting adaptation to local conditions. Redundancy analysis and Mantel test identified dissolved oxygen, ammonium, and nitrogen species as key environmental filters. Functional prediction suggested enrichment of fermentative and methanogenic pathways in anaerobic zones, while nitrification and photoautotrophy dominated downstream. Forty-six taxa assigned as potential bacterial pathogens were detected, including World Health Organization (WHO)-priority species such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila. While K. pneumoniae was substantially reduced (up to 77.9%), its persistence-along with L. pneumophila detection in the final effluent-highlights reuse-associated risks. This study provides system-specific insights into the prokaryotic community dynamics, predicted functional stratification, and potential pathogen attenuation in a full-scale WSP system, emphasizing the need for targeted prokaryotic monitoring and improved management strategies to ensure biosafe and sustainable wastewater reuse.

papers.title: Phylogenetic analysis of the cpn60 UT region identifies conserved oligonucleotide regions for Enterobacterales detection.
papers.abstract: T​he members of Enterobacterales order cause a wide range of gastrointestinal and other mucosal infections when contaminated food and water are consumed. Conventional microbiological methods for detecting these pathogens are laborious and are time-consuming. Molecular assays offer a fast and sensitive pathogen detection, but identifying a reliable target gene is essential for the assay development. In this study, we explored the cpn60 universal target (UT) region as a potential target for detecting Enterobacterales including Escherichia coli, Shigella​, Salmonella, Proteus and Klebsiella sp. We performed phylogenetic analysis of cpn60​ UT region ​among the Enterobacterales. This analysis revealed the presence of 13 clusters and two oligonucleotide regions with the highest nucleotide conservation. Targeting these regions, we designed a set of oligonucleotide primer pairs and developed ​a SYBR Green real-time PCR (qPCR) assay to detect the Enterobacterales members. The degenerate primers amplified a 132 bp fragment within​ the cpn60​ UT region across Enterobacterales. The analytical sensitivity of​ assay was initially investigated using the thermal lysates from 10-fold serial dilution of overnight broth culture of E. coli ATCC 10536 and achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 10 1 CFU/mL. Assay specificity was assessed across Enterobacterales and non-Enterobacterales control strains, including Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) and Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes).

papers.title: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. juglandis Affecting Walnut in California: Population Genomics, Copper Resistance, and Type III Effectors.
papers.abstract: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. juglandis ( Xaj ), causal agent of walnut blight, remains a threat to crop production throughout California growing regions, and the efficacy of copper-based bactericides is often compromised due to widespread resistance in the pathogen. Despite the economic impact of this pathogen on California walnut production, little is known about its population structure, phenotypic variability, genetic mechanisms for copper resistance, and type III secretion system effector (T3E) repertoires. Whole-genome sequencing and de novo genome assembly were conducted using 115 strains from 12 counties. Population structure and phylogenetic relationships were assessed based on recombination-corrected core-genome alignments. Six genetic clusters were identified, but no correlation between cluster assignment and geographic origin was found. Phylogenetic reconstruction that included 24 global strains revealed distinct clades composed exclusively of California Xaj , whereas other clades also contained strains from other countries, and one only included global strains. A pangenome approach facilitated the identification of copper resistance operons encoded within distinct mobile genetic elements, suggesting that copper resistance likely evolved independently multiple times in the population. Seventy-seven Xaj strains harbored copper resistance operons, and in vitro assays confirmed that those strains were copper-resistant. The California Xaj population encoded between 17 and 22 T3Es, with variation observed among strains from different genetic clusters. Additional putative type I to IV secretion system effectors were predicted using a pretrained protein language model. Together, these findings revealed moderate genetic and effector diversity coupled with widespread copper resistance in the California Xaj population and generated high-quality genomic resources to advance Xanthomonas research.

papers.title: Hydrogel-Embedded Precision-Cut Lung Slices Enable Controlled Biochemical Stimulation and Dynamic Matrix Stiffening to Recapitulate Features of Pulmonary Fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) retain the native cells and extracellular matrix that contribute to the structural and functional integrity of lung tissue. This technique enables the study of cell-matrix interactions and is particularly useful for pre-clinical pharmacological studies. More specifically, PCLS are widely used to model the complex pathophysiology of pulmonary fibrosis, an uncurable and progressive interstitial lung disease. Current ex vivo pulmonary fibrosis models expose PCLS to pro-fibrotic biochemical cues over a short timeframe (hours to days) and quickly collect samples for analysis due to viability concerns. This condensed timeline is a limitation to understanding chronic disease mechanisms. To extend the utility of ex vivo pulmonary fibrosis models, PCLS were embedded in engineered hydrogels and exposed to pro-fibrotic biochemical and biophysical cues. Hydrogel-embedded PCLS maintained greater than 80% total cell viability over 3 weeks in culture. Pro-fibrotic biochemical and mechanical cues induced gene- and protein-level changes associated with fibrotic remodeling. Finally, treatment with the FDA-approved anti-fibrotic drug Nintedanib produced a coordinated response across multiple transcriptional and protein-level endpoints. Collectively, these results show that hydrogel-embedded PCLS models of pulmonary fibrosis extend our ability to study fibrotic processes ex vivo and, when applied to human tissues, present a new approach methodology for studying lung disease and treatment. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating, incurable chronic lung disease characterized by progressive scarring, increased tissue stiffness, and loss of lung function. Current treatments slow disease progression but do not reverse established fibrosis. In this study, precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) were embedded in engineered biomaterial hydrogels to create an extended-culture platform for investigating fibrotic processes in intact lung tissue. Hydrogels were dynamically stiffened to reproduce mechanical features of fibrosis, while PCLS were independently exposed to pro-fibrotic biochemical cues. Together, these inputs induced fibrosis-associated changes in extracellular matrix deposition, gene expression, and protein abundance while maintaining tissue viability over multiple weeks. Treatment with the FDA-approved anti-fibrotic drug Nintedanib produced a coordinated response across multiple transcriptional and protein-level endpoints. This dynamically tunable biomaterial-tissue platform enables investigation of biochemical and mechanical contributions to pulmonary fibrosis and provides a foundation for therapeutic evaluation in intact lung tissue.

papers.title: Heat Shock Proteinsshock proteins in Parkinson's disease: A dynamic continuum from neuroprotection to pathology.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, is pathologically defined by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) into Lewy bodies, which spread from the nigrostriatal system to the olfactory bulb, lower brainstem, limbic regions, and ultimately the cerebral cortex. Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are a group of essential molecular chaperones maintaining proteostasis in this disease. However, their roles are far more complicated than previous researchers considered. This is not a simple dichotomy. We argue that HSPs are neither intrinsically protective nor pathogenic; instead, they exist on a dynamic continuum shaped by disease stage, ATP supply, and the integrity of the co-chaperone network. We propose that HSPs' functional shifts in PD may be stage-dependent: HSC70/HSP70-mediated compensatory clearance predominates in early phases, clearing misfolded/aggregated α-synuclein by inhibiting aggregation and promoting degradation to maintain protein homeostasis. In later stages of the disease, PD pathology leads to ATP depletion and co-chaperone network imbalance, shifting HSPs' function toward HSP90-driven pathogenic mechanisms. This framework moves HSPs from a binary classification to a dynamic, stage-sensitive model, with direct implications for trial design and therapeutic timing. However, a systematic overview dynamic role for HSPs remains lacking. Here, we synthesize evidence on both the protective and pathogenic roles of HSPs in PD, providing proposed ideas for a theoretical foundation for developing rational, HSP-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Molecular Characteristics and Antimicrobial Resistance of Vibrio parahaemolyticus Isolated from Aquatic Products in Huzhou, China.
papers.abstract: Vibrio parahaemolyticus (V. parahaemolyticus) is a major pathogen responsible for seafood-associated gastroenteritis worldwide. In recent years, the number of infections caused by this bacterium has shown a significant increasing trend globally. In this study, antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequencing were performed on 150 strains of V. parahaemolyticus isolated from 1,111 aquatic product samples collected in Huzhou area in 2025. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST), resistance gene profiling, virulence gene analysis, and genetic relatedness assessment were conducted using bioinformatics approaches. A total of 23 serotypes were identified among the 150 strains, with the most common being O2:KUT (18.00%), O2:K28 (13.30%), and O1:KUT (12.67%). The 150 strains were classified into 81 sequence types (STs), showing a relatively scattered distribution. The strains exhibited varying degrees of resistance to most antibiotics, with the highest resistance rate observed against colistin (CT, 84.00%). Multidrug resistance was frequently observed among the isolates in this study. A total of 31 resistance-related genes belonging to nine classes were detected, with β-lactam resistance genes being predominant. Additionally, 192 virulence genes were identified; all isolates carried the tlh gene, but neither tdh nor trh was detected. Furthermore, all isolates carried effector proteins associated with T3SS1. Phylogenetic analysis based on core gene trees indicated that serotyping was highly correlated with the genetic background of the core genome, and the strains exhibited a multi-branch, multi-lineage co-existing structure across geographical regions and isolation sources, without forming a single predominant clonal group.Huzhou seafood V. parahaemolyticus shows high cephalosporin/multidrug resistance and genetic heterogeneity; all lacked tdh/trh but carried T3SS1, so resistance and virulence genomics should inform risk monitoring.

papers.title: Comparative Genomics of Complete Genomes from Non-Kp1 Species within the Klebsiella pneumoniae Species Complex: A Hidden Reservoir of Carbapenem Resistance and Virulence.
papers.abstract: The Klebsiella pneumoniae species complex (KpSC) poses a global public health threat, yet genomic studies have disproportionately focused on Klebsiella pneumoniae (Kp1), leaving the clinical and epidemiological significance of non-Kp1 species less underexplored. In this study, we analyzed a selected collection of complete genomes to identify genomic determinants associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence across non-Kp1 Klebsiella species. We retrieved complete non-Kp1 genomes from the NCBI database and retained 340 assemblies after stringent quality assessment. Comprehensive comparative genomic analyses were performed, encompassing distribution, phylogenomics, resistome and virulome profiling, plasmid typing, pan-genome characterization, and the genetic contexts of carbapenemase genes. Analysis of the 340 high-quality assemblies identified Klebsiella variicola subsp. variicola (Kp3) as the dominant lineage (51.5%). Klebsiella quasipneumoniae subsp. quasipneumoniae (Kp2) exhibited a high carbapenemase gene carriage (44.1%). The IncF family was the most prevalent plasmid replicon type. Phylogenomics suggested a genomic overlap across ecological distribution. Pan-genome analysis identified 129 significantly enriched genes in non-Kp1, primarily enriched in inorganic ion transport, transcription, and signal transduction. Carbapenemase genetic environments closely paralleled those found in prevalent Kp1 clones: bla KPC-2 was located within the canonical transposonTn4401; bla NDM-1 was part of a highly conserved genetic array (bla NDM-1 -ble-trpF-dsbD-cutA-groS-groL); and bla OXA-181 was conserved on a disseminated IncX3-type plasmid backbone. Non-Kp1 species may serve as potential cross-sectoral dissemination for resistance and virulence determinants, harboring traits with genomic signatures parallel to Kp1 via shared mobile genetic elements. Their metabolic specialization is hypothesized to potentially facilitate environmental persistence. These findings suggest that enhanced molecular diagnostics and integrated One Health surveillance are essential to better characterize the dissemination of these species.

papers.title: Post-COVID-19 age-distribution dynamics and symptom reporting patterns of respiratory pathogens: a direct-to-consumer surveillance study of nearly one million tests in China, 2023 -2025.
papers.abstract: To assess post-COVID-19 age-specific detection and symptom reporting patterns of respiratory pathogens to inform surveillance strategies. Utilizing direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing data from 975,107 community tests across four Chinese regions (October 2023-October 2025), we analyzed the epidemic patterns, temporal changes in age distribution of positive tests, and age-specific symptom reporting rates for seven respiratory pathogens. Generalized additive models (GAM) and spline regression were employed to analyze temporal and age-dependent trends. The standardized age percentile of positive tests decreased by an average of 0.37 and 1.01 percentage points per month for influenza A virus (IFV-A) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), respectively, indicating a shift toward younger age groups, whereas it increased by 0.27 percentage points per month for human rhinovirus (HRV), indicating a shift toward older age groups. Symptom reporting was highly age-dependent. Fever reporting for IFV-A/influenza B virus (IFV-B)/human adenovirus (HAdV) showed an "L-shaped" decline with age (child pattern), whereas RSV and SARS-CoV-2 showed a "V-shaped" rebound in the elderly (child-elderly pattern). Respiratory and pain symptoms generally peaked in adulthood (inverted V-shaped, adult pattern), except HAdV-related respiratory symptoms (inverted L-shaped, elderly pattern). Post-COVID-19 age distribution dynamics are divergent and pathogen-specific. The marked age dependency of symptom profiles, together with lower reporting of classic symptoms among older adults, suggests that fever-centric surveillance case definitions may contribute to under-recognition of respiratory infections in older adults. These findings support age-stratified surveillance and optimized case definitions to guide targeted prevention and control.

papers.title: SurvStudio for browser-based survival analysis and model comparison in cancer genomics.
papers.abstract: Molecular prognostic studies need to test whether markers improve prediction beyond clinical variables. This requires survival analysis, model comparison and checks of data coding and model assumptions, steps that existing tools often provide separately. We developed SurvStudio to combine survival analysis, marker assessment and machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) model comparison in one browser workspace. SurvStudio analyzes prepared clinical and molecular tables and compares models in the same test patients. Users install SurvStudio locally and run it through a web browser. We evaluated it using synthetic data and public cancer cohorts and compared its outputs with existing tools. Browser controls provided survival curves, clinically adjusted marker estimates, selection-stability summaries and comparison of nine prediction models. Fixed marker models could also be applied to external cohorts. Adding established isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation/1p/19q codeletion groups to age, sex and grade increased the concordance index (C) of the primary gradient-boosting model in two external glioma cohorts (ΔC = 0.118 and 0.084, 95% confidence intervals 0.067-0.171 and 0.035-0.136). The nine models had similar C values (0.632-0.646) in 381 breast cancer test patients. Input checks blocked specified invalid inputs and asked users to review predictors that may contain outcome information. In a public gastric cancer cohort, correct event coding changed estimated five-year survival from 89.3% to 52.2%. With SurvStudio, researchers can test whether molecular markers improve survival prediction beyond clinical variables and compare survival models in one browser workspace, while input checks and model diagnostics show whether the data and models support each result.

papers.title: Challenges and opportunities in antimicrobial R&D.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is accelerating, while the discovery and development of new drugs, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action, have failed to keep pace. This widening gap reflects two major challenges: insufficient resources for antibiotic discovery and clinical development, and a lack of scientific innovation. With pharmaceutical companies largely abandoning antibiotic R&D, academic groups, small biotech companies, and not-for-profits are stepping in, harnessing advances in genomics, synthetic biology, and AI to drive discovery. Coupled with growing international investment and initiatives to address funding gaps, these efforts offer renewed hope for overcoming the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

papers.title: Beyond the Chatbot: Agentic Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Infectious Disease Practice.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) discourse in infectious disease (ID) has focused on benchmarking large language model chatbots against clinicians, a useful but narrowing inquiry. Agentic AI is a different paradigm: goal-directed systems that pursue clinical objectives over time, integrating data, invoking tools, monitoring results, and adapting without repeated prompting. This Viewpoint defines the anatomy of an agent, situates it within a 3-level framework (predictive, conversational, agentic), and examines how agents could transform 6 domains of ID practice: clinical care, antimicrobial stewardship, clinical microbiology, infection prevention and control, research, and epidemiology and pandemic preparedness. Individual components have proven value; integrated systems remain untested. No validated agentic system has been deployed in clinical ID; error propagation, algorithmic bias, cost, absent validation frameworks, undefined liability, and consequences for the workforce and its training must be addressed first. The ID community has a narrow window to shape these systems before decisions are made without it.

papers.title: Cas12a Autocatalytic Amplification Coupled with a DNA-Regulated COF Nanozyme Activation for the Colorimetric Detection of Staphylococcus aureus.
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a major foodborne and clinical pathogen, and its rapid and accurate detection are essential for food safety monitoring and clinical diagnostics. Here, we developed a colorimetric platform for quantifying S. aureus that integrates circular DNA (Cir-DNA)-mediated Cas12a autocatalytic amplification with DNA regulation of a covalent organic framework (COFTph-BT) nanozyme. Recognition of the 16S rDNA target by the Cas12a/crRNA complex activates trans-cleavage activity, which linearizes Cir-DNA and initiates an autocatalytic amplification circuit that drives cascade cleavage of probe S1. Signal transduction exploits the differential binding affinities of COFTph-BT for single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), and its peroxidase activities could be reversely regulated by the surface modification of ssDNA. Cleavage of S1 inhibits its hybridization with COFTph-BT surface-bound S2, maintaining S2 predominantly in its single-stranded form and preserving the catalytic activity of COFTph-BT-S2. The nanozyme subsequently catalyzes the oxidation of colorless 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) to blue oxidized TMB (oxTMB), generating a colorimetric readout. The assay can be completed within 90 min and achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 7 CFU mL-1. Integration with smartphone-based image analysis further enables portable colorimetric detection with an LOD of 87 CFU mL-1. This strategy provides an approach for the sensitive colorimetric detection of foodborne pathogens, with potential applications in food safety monitoring and clinical diagnostics.

papers.title: Database resources of the National Center for Biotechnology Information in 2027.
papers.abstract: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) provides biomedical data resources including PubMed®, a repository of citations and abstracts published in life science journals, and ClinicalTrials.gov, a repository of clinical research summaries. NCBI also hosts a multitude of resources providing nucleotide sequences and sequence-derived products, such as proteins and protein structures. Search and retrieval operations are available for most of the 40 distinct repositories, knowledgebases, and services. The E-utilities and NCBI Datasets serve as the programming interface for most of these. Resources receiving significant updates in the past year include PubMed®, PubMed Central® (PMC), SciENcv, ClinicalTrials.gov, ClinVar, dbSNP, dbGaP, GTR, MedGen®, Pathogen Detection and the National Database of Antibiotic Resistant Organisms, and PubChem®. These resources can be accessed through the NCBI home page at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov.

papers.title: Genomic rearrangement of the capsule operon in a phylogenetically distinct cluster of the multi-drug-resistant Escherichia coli lineage ST131.
papers.abstract: Escherichia coli ST131 is a dominant cause of multi-drug-resistant extraintestinal infections in humans. The lineage has a three-clade phylogenetic structure, of which clade C has gained resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics and is globally disseminated. As well as antimicrobial resistance, a number of virulence factors contribute to the success of ST131 clade C, including the production of capsule. Previous work on a limited number of strains has shown that the capsule operon in ST131 is highly variable. In this study, we analyzed the capsule genetics of E. coli ST131 by interrogating 3,033 genomes. Our data show a clonal distribution of capsule types and identify a monophyletic group of ST131 clade C strains that are characterized by an atypical capsule operon with highly divergent alleles of the key kpsM and kpsT genes. Our analysis suggests there is ongoing evolution within clade C of ST131, which looks to be driven not by the continuing evolution of antimicrobial resistance but by host-pathogen interactions.IMPORTANCEMulti-drug-resistant (MDR) Escherichia coli is a problematic cause of invasive disease in humans and animals. Resistance to multiple classes of antibiotics is severely limiting treatment options. ST131-C is a highly successful, MDR clone of E. coli that is a major cause of extraintestinal infections. Capsule is a key virulence factor in contributing to this clone's success, with capsule switching allowing the bacteria flexibility to thrive in different niches. We present evidence that suggests continual evolution of this proliferant clone influenced by host-pathogen interaction. Small genetic changes can define the success of a clone; therefore, it is important to monitor this continual evolution in pathogens.

papers.title: Natural variation of hypervirulent Klebsiella pathogenicity loci among Taiwan bloodstream isolates.
papers.abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major cause of both nosocomial and community-acquired infections, with hypervirulent (hvKP) strains causing severe disease in healthy individuals. In Southeastern Asia, diabetes mellitus is a recognized risk factor for hvKP-associated pyogenic liver abscesses. hvKP virulence is typically attributed to carriage of a large virulence plasmid encoding siderophore biosynthesis ( iuc , iro ) and mucoid regulator ( rmpA , rmpA2 ) genes. Here, we analyzed 50 bloodstream isolates from Taipei, Taiwan, to investigate genomic and phenotypic characteristics of isolates from patients with or without diabetes mellitus. In diabetic patients and patients with liver abscesses, hvKP biomarkers were found in 66% ( n = 33) and 64% ( n = 32) of isolates, respectively. While we expected hvKP isolates to be overrepresented in this collection, we observed extensive diversity among hvKP pathogenicity loci, with strains of typical ST23 hvKP lineages carrying incomplete KpVP-1 virulence plasmids. This hvKP biomarker diversity is typically found in classical multidrug-resistant lineages that have acquired portions of the virulence plasmid. Phenotypic assays showed that hvKP biomarkers did not strictly predict hypermucoviscosity, capsule and siderophore production, or survival in serum. Loss of rmpA consistently eliminated hypermucoviscosity and reduced virulence in a murine pneumonia model, whereas aerobactin loss did not. In vivo studies demonstrated variations in virulence that could not be explained solely by differences in the number of hypervirulence-associated loci. These findings highlight the complexity of K. pneumoniae pathogenesis and demonstrate that while canonical biomarkers effectively distinguish hvKP from classical K. pneumoniae , they are insufficient to predict variation in virulence among hvKP strains. Our findings provide insight into the virulence spectrum of strains carrying incomplete plasmid configurations.IMPORTANCE K. pneumoniae poses a global health threat due to the convergence of antimicrobial resistance and hypervirulence. We identified substantial diversity in virulence plasmid content, including incomplete virulence plasmids within archetypal hvKP lineages, and showed that phenotypic and in vivo virulence traits cannot be fully explained by the presence or absence of individual hypervirulence-associated loci. While canonical biomarkers such as rmpA and iuc are widely used to distinguish hypervirulent strains, our analysis demonstrates that no single biomarker is sufficient to reliably predict pathogenic potential and that virulence depends on specific locus combinations and broader context. These findings highlight a critical gap in our understanding of hvKP pathogenesis, underscoring the need for more nuanced frameworks to evaluate virulence. This work has important implications for clinical diagnostics, surveillance, and risk assessment of emerging K. pneumoniae strains worldwide.

papers.title: Integrated Management of Rose Downy Mildew ( Peronospora sparsa ): Linking Epidemiology to Disease Control.
papers.abstract: Downy mildew, caused by the oomycete Peronospora sparsa , is a major constraint in rose ( Rosa spp.) production, particularly under conditions of prolonged leaf wetness and high humidity. Although substantial progress has been made in understanding pathogen biology, fungicide performance, and detection methods, the translation of epidemiological knowledge into practical disease management remains poorly developed. This review synthesizes recent advances (2020 to 2025) in rose downy mildew research, with emphasis on linking infection dynamics to actionable control strategies. Cultural practices that regulate canopy microclimate such as ventilation, irrigation timing, and plant spacing, together with targeted fungicide applications, remain the most reliable control measures. In contrast, biological control agents and host resistance strategies show promise but lack consistent validation under commercial production conditions. Recent molecular studies have improved understanding of host-pathogen interactions, although their direct application in management remains limited. Based on current evidence, we propose an integrated pest management framework that combines environmental monitoring, infection risk assessment, and optimized fungicide use to improve control efficacy in both field and protected systems. Key research priorities include the development of predictive models and validation of integrated strategies under diverse production conditions. In particular, integrating epidemiological thresholds such as leaf wetness duration and humidity into decision-based management frameworks is essential for improving the timing and effectiveness of disease control interventions.

papers.title: Subtractive Genomic Approach for Identification of Pathogen-Specific Essential Genes as Target and Drug Repurposing in Major Foodborne Bacteria.
papers.abstract: Foodborne diseases pose a substantial threat to global public health and economic stability, with bacterial contamination occurring at multiple stages of the food supply chain. The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among foodborne pathogens has further complicated the prevention and treatment of these infections, underscoring the urgent need for novel, pathogen-specific therapeutic targets. In this study, a comprehensive subtractive genomics approach was employed to systematically identify bacterial key genes (bKGs) as drug targets and to explore corresponding potential therapeutic agents. Seven major foodborne bacteria, Listeria monocytogenes , Campylobacter jejuni , Staphylococcus aureus , Clostridium perfringens , Escherichia coli O157:H7, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, and Shigella sonnei , were selected for the subtractive genomic analysis. Initially, paralogous proteins and proteins homologous to the human host were eliminated to obtain pathogen-specific proteins, which were subsequently screened against the Database of Essential Genes (DEG) to identify essential genes. Functional annotation through metabolic pathway analysis and subcellular localization provided insights into their biological roles. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis identified five hub proteins per pathogen, yielding a total of 35 hub proteins. Further network centrality analysis revealed seven conserved hub-of-hub proteins, dnaK , leuS , rplC , rplJ , rpoA , rpsC , and rpsD , as critical for bacterial survival and pathogenicity. A set of 88 drugs targeting foodborne pathogens was collected from the literature and subjected to molecular docking against the selected hub-of-hub proteins. Notably, dnaK showed the strongest binding affinity with Domperidone (-9.9 kcal/mol), leuS with Netupitant (-8.9 kcal/mol), and rpoA with Rifaximin (-7.0 kcal/mol). These candidate drugs also exhibited favorable toxicity profiles and predicted biological activity. Therefore, this study provides a robust computational framework for identifying pathogen-specific essential genes and repurposable drug candidates, offering valuable insights for the development of targeted therapies against foodborne bacterial infections and contributing to efforts to combat AMR and improve food safety.

papers.title: Apparently Homozygous Germline CDKN2A Variant in a Patient With Multiple Primary Melanomas.
papers.abstract: Germline heterozygous variants in CDKN2A are a major cause of familial melanoma, whereas constitutional biallelic variants remain extremely rare and poorly characterized. We report a 33-year-old man with multiple primary melanomas who subsequently developed metastatic disease requiring immunotherapy and was found to carry an apparently homozygous missense variant (c.71G>C, p.Arg24Pro) in the CDKN2A gene. Whole-genome sequencing highlighted a 1.0-Mb region of homozygosity on Chromosome 9 encompassing CDKN2A and targeted testing demonstrated that the proband's mother was heterozygous for the same variant, confirming maternal transmission of one allele, whereas the proband's father was deceased and unavailable for testing. The variant is classified as likely pathogenic according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics criteria and has previously been shown to impair binding to CDK4. A comparative review of previously reported individuals with constitutional biallelic CDKN2A variants highlights substantial phenotypic heterogeneity, ranging from early-onset multiple primary melanomas to phenotypes overlapping with those observed in heterozygous carriers. This report expands the limited literature on constitutional biallelic CDKN2A mutation but does not allow conclusions to be drawn regarding genotype-phenotype correlations or gene-dosage effects. Additional well-characterized cases are required to clarify the clinical consequences of constitutional biallelic variants in CDKN2A .

papers.title: Species-Specific Responses to Snake Fungal Disease: Effects on Space Use, Detection, and Density in Two Semi-Aquatic Natricine Species.
papers.abstract: Wildlife diseases pose increasing threats to reptiles, and evaluating the population-level impacts is often challenging due to the cryptic nature and low detectability of many species. Snake Fungal Disease (SFD or ophidiomycosis), caused by the fungal pathogen Ophidiomyces ophidiicola , has emerged as a potential threat to snake populations, yet few studies have documented population declines directly linked to the disease. We utilized 3 years of passive integrated transponder tag telemetry, disease monitoring, and multi-session spatial capture-recapture models to investigate the effects of snake fungal disease on population densities, spatial scale of detection values, and detection probabilities of Common Watersnake ( Nerodia sipedon ) and Queensnake ( Regina septemvittata ) populations in three central Kentucky streams. We hypothesized that SFD would alter population density over time and that SFD-related physiological impairment or behavioral change would result in species-specific changes in space use and detection probability. Density estimates declined across most sites and sessions over the study period, although these declines were generally not statistically significant, and we could not link them to differences in prevalence rates between sites. Infected N. sipedon exhibited significantly smaller spatial scale of detection values compared to non-infected individuals, whereas no significant differences were observed in R. septemvittata . Infection status did not affect the detection probability of either species, but N. sipedon detection probability increased with day of year, and R. septemvittata detection probability increased with rain accumulation between survey periods. These results indicate that SFD may pose an ongoing risk to snake population stability and can produce sublethal, species-specific effects on space use well before potential population declines and highlight the need for long-term monitoring programs that integrate multiple survey methods and emerging technologies to enhance detection probability and population-level inference.

papers.title: Civilization, assisted reproduction, and the human genome: from relaxed selection to technological correction.
papers.abstract: Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) are now a structural component of reproduction in high-income societies, yet their population-level genetic and clinical consequences remain incompletely characterised. This structured narrative review integrates evolutionary genetics, reproductive epidemiology, ART outcomes, and bioethics. Evidence is strongest for paternal-age-associated de novo mutations, expanded carrier screening (ECS), preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M), and the limitations of testing for polygenic disorders (PGT-P). Moderate, direct but limited adult offspring evidence suggests that intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) used for paternal male-factor infertility can permit intergenerational transmission of infertility-associated phenotypes. ART-associated imprinting and methylation evidence is moderate but confounded by parental subfertility. Repeated donor use may concentrate pathogenic variants; delayed childbearing selection on ovarian reserve and laboratory-derived chemical exposures remain hypothesis-generating. ECS and PGT-M primarily reduce affected pregnancies or births among identified at-risk couples; they do not directly remove carrier alleles or demonstrate a reduction in population mutation load. The population genetic and clinical impact of modern reproduction therefore depends on practice and policy. Coupling ART with ECS, accessible PGT-M and donor governance may reduce preventable inherited disease while preserving reproductive autonomy.

papers.title: Replicon-based antiviral screening identifies Simeprevir and Mosnodenvir as inhibitors of Kyasanur Forest Disease virus.
papers.abstract: Kyasanur Forest Disease virus (KFDV) is an emerging tick-borne flavivirus endemic to India. Currently, molecular studies and antiviral development for KFDV have been hindered by the need for high-containment laboratories to work with the infectious virus and by a lack of simple BSL-2-compatible replicon systems. In this study, we have developed a BSL-2-compatible KFDV sub-genomic replicon that supports viral RNA replication without producing infectious virions. The replicon encodes a Renilla luciferase reporter in place of the structural genes and was stabilized in a bacterial artificial chromosome to overcome plasmid instability associated with flaviviral genomes. Replication competence was validated in BHK-21 cells through luciferase assays, strand-specific RT-PCR, and detection of double-stranded RNA replication intermediates. Using this platform, we screened a panel of anti-flaviviral compounds and identified Ribavirin, Dasabuvir, Simeprevir, and Mosnodenvir as inhibitors of KFDV replication. Dose-response analyses revealed potent antiviral activity for Simeprevir (IC 50 = 4.88 μM) and Mosnodenvir (IC 50 = 2.22 μM). Antiviral activity was subsequently confirmed using infectious KFDV, where both compounds reduced viral RNA levels and infectious virus titers. Molecular docking studies suggested distinct mechanisms of inhibition, with Simeprevir potentially acting through allosteric inhibition of NS3 and Mosnodenvir targeting a conserved NS4B binding pocket. Together, these findings establish a robust antiviral screening platform for KFDV and identify promising therapeutics against this emerging pathogen.

papers.title: Diagnostic value and report-anchored antimicrobial prescribing changes following BALF targeted next-generation sequencing in lower respiratory tract infections: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Comprehensive evidence on the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) in lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remains limited. We evaluated its diagnostic and antimicrobial management value in routine clinical practice. This retrospective cohort study included 433 patients hospitalized with suspected LRTIs at Wuhan First Hospital between February and June 2026. tNGS performance was assessed by pathogen detection profiles, concordance with culture, clinical relevance and antimicrobial prescribing changes within 72 hours of report availability. Within the matched detection spectrum, tNGS detection rate was substantially higher than culture (87.1% vs. 40.2%), with a median of three organisms per report. Higher read counts were associated with a greater likelihood of organism-matched culture positivity. Against the composite clinical adjudication reference, positive tNGS findings had an overall PPV of 89.7%, which was higher for bacterial than fungal detections (92.8% vs. 18.4%). Within 72 h of report availability, 207 patients had regimen modifications; 74.4% were considered mainly or partly supported by tNGS. Among evaluable tNGS-concordant regimens, subsequent AST provided additional support in 69.7%. BALF tNGS broadened microbial detection beyond culture and was associated with early antimicrobial modification. Integrating RPM, culture, AST, and report timing may enhance diagnostic interpretation and clinical actionability.

papers.title: CRC tumor antigens and immune escape: Designing peptide vaccines for colorectal Cancer.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality, with current therapies often limited by toxicity and resistance. Immunotherapy, particularly peptide-based vaccines, represents a promising alternative by eliciting targeted immune responses. This review provides a critical and comparative synthesis of CRC peptide vaccine development, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating mechanistic insights into immune evasion with a structured framework that connects antigen selection, epitope identification (experimental and computational), and clinical translation. We specifically highlight two underexplored areas: tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) and the critical distinction between microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC, which fundamentally dictates mutational burden, neoantigen load, and vaccine responsiveness. We first detail the sophisticated mechanisms of immune evasion employed by CRC, including an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment enriched with regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), dysregulated antigen presentation via HLA class I alterations, and expression of inhibitory checkpoints. The review critically evaluates methods for epitope identification, contrasting traditional experimental approaches with modern computational strategies that leverage genomics, AI, and immunoinformatics tools for predicting high-affinity, immunogenic epitopes. We emphasize that predicted immunogenicity does not equate to clinical efficacy, and we critically appraise the limitations of current computational tools, including high false-positive rates and poor correlation with in vivo immunogenicity. While promising, challenges remain, including low immunogenicity, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) restriction, and tumor heterogeneity. Future success likely depends on developing multi-epitope, personalized vaccines combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance efficacy. In conclusion, peptide vaccines offer a precise and adaptable platform for CRC immunotherapy, holding significant potential for improving clinical outcomes through targeted immune activation.

papers.title: Preclinical evaluation of an adaptable single-cycle SARS-CoV-2 vaccine against XBB.1.5 in mice and hamsters.
papers.abstract: A next-generation SARS-CoV-2 vaccine must address the currently inadequate prevention of virus transmission, particularly against emerging variants of concern, a challenge that none of the licenced commercial vaccines fully meet. Effective control of respiratory pandemics necessitates vaccines that 1) can be rapidly adapted, 2) have high patient compliance with simple and non-invasive administration, and 3) block transmission following virus challenge. We describe the characterization of an updated single-cycle SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate (scVac), engineered as a replication-defective virus with targeted deletions of the E gene and ORF6 and ORF7a, together with a truncation of ORF3a. The candidate carries an Omicron XBB.1.5 Spike (scVac XBB ), while maintaining all essential antigenic properties. Safety was evaluated in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, the most sensitive virulence model, and immunogenicity and efficacy were assessed in the Syrian hamster model. The vaccine was well tolerated in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, with no clinical signs or adverse events observed. In Syrian hamsters, scVac XBB induced potent systemic and mucosal immune responses, together with a strong neutralising antibody response. Notably, no virus transmission to co-housed naïve animals was detected in the scVac-vaccinated group. In contrast, transmission was observed in the bivalent Omicron mRNA vaccine comparator group under the conditions tested. Our results demonstrate that scVac XBB -induced immunity not only prevents disease but also transmission in a prime-boost hamster direct-contact model following homologous XBB.1.5 challenge. Furthermore, the successful incorporation of the XBB.1.5 Spike protein into the scVac frame supports its potential for adaptation to emerging variants. These findings highlight the potential of this single-cycle vaccine concept as a next-generation COVID-19 vaccine, offering robust protection, effective interruption of transmission, and a favourable tolerability observed in the evaluated animal models. Research was funded by the German Research Foundation, an Innosuisse grant, and by RocketVax AG.

papers.title: Genomic characterization of a novel WVMV isolate and development of a sensitive, field-deployable RT-RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a lateral flow detection assay.
papers.abstract: Wisteria vein mosaic virus (WVMV), a potyviral pathogen, severely compromises the ornamental quality of wisteria plants, yet conventional diagnostic tools fail to support rapid on-site screening under field conditions. Herein, we characterized a novel WVMV isolate designated WVMV-GZWf, recovered from symptomatic wisteria foliage in Guizhou Province, China.
